title: How to frame a cross-stitch piece
subtitle: Preparing and mounting finished stitching in a picture frame
excerpt: Framing a cross-stitch piece protects the stitching, displays it flat, and gives it a finished appearance on a wall. The piece is pressed, then mounted over a piece of card or foam board and laced or taped on the back to keep it taut and straight inside the frame. Glass or acrylic glazing keeps dust off the surface.
sourceNotes: Framing guidance for cross-stitch. Standard guidance in major cross-stitch publisher guides and needlework finishing resources.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads.
The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch.

content.text: Framing a cross-stitch piece correctly means the
is mounted taut and flat with the grid square to the frame edges, and the
is not compressed against the glazing. UV-protective glass or acrylic is preferred to protect the thread colours from fading over time.
Press the finished piece from the back on a padded surface. The Aida should be flat and smooth, with no hoop marks or distortion.
Cut a piece of acid-free mount board or foam board to fit the back of the frame's glazing. The board should fill the frame aperture exactly, with no gaps at the edges.

Centre the stitched piece face down on the board, checking that the design is centred and that the Aida grid runs square to the board edges. Pull the fabric taut over the board edges and hold it in place on the back with pins pushed into the board's edge.

Lace the fabric in place using a strong thread: run a long thread horizontally across the back of the board, threading it through the fabric edge at intervals and pulling it taut at each pass. Tie off and repeat vertically. Lacing is more stable than adhesive tape over time and does not damage the fabric.

Assemble the frame: place the mounted piece face up inside the frame, with the glazing in front and a backing board behind. Fix the backing in place with frame points or tape. The piece should be firm and the design should be centred and straight when viewed from the front.

items.symptom: The design is not centred in the frame opening
items.cause: The piece was not centred on the mount board before lacing.
items.fix: Unlace, reposition the Aida on the board with the design centred, re-pin at the corners, and re-lace. Check centring from the front before tying off the lacing thread.

items.symptom: The glazing is pressing against the stitches and flattening them
items.cause: There is no mount or gap between the glazing and the stitched surface.
items.fix: Add a card mount (a card frame with a cut window) between the glazing and the stitching. This holds the glazing away from the fabric surface and prevents the stitches from being compressed. A standard pre-cut mount from a framing supplier usually fits standard frame sizes.

content.text: A professional framer can lace and mount the piece for you if the lacing step is unfamiliar. Most picture framers who handle embroidery will know the process. If you do the framing yourself, the investment in acid-free board and UV-protective glazing protects the piece for decades rather than years.
